DOCUMENT:
Pricing Proposal: Weekend Rate Restructure
Harbourside Hotel, Revenue Management, April 2026

1. Proposal
From 1 June 2026 we propose to (a) raise the Best Available Rate (BAR) for Friday and Saturday nights from £145 to £165, and (b) introduce a two-night minimum for any stay that includes a Saturday night. Midweek rates are unchanged.

2. Context
Harbourside is a 112-room four-star hotel on the quay, with a leisure-led weekend business and a corporate-led midweek business. Our weekend BAR is £20 to £35 below the three comparable hotels in our competitive set, whose weekend rates currently range from £165 to £180. Weekend occupancy has recovered strongly since 2023 and we believe we are leaving money on the table.

Table 1. Weekend (Friday and Saturday) occupancy by month, 2025
Jan 62% | Feb 66% | Mar 74% | Apr 80% | May 85% | Jun 81%
Jul 89% | Aug 93% | Sep 88% | Oct 82% | Nov 72% | Dec 78%

Average weekend occupancy across 2025 was 79%. July and August are our strongest months, driven by the harbour festival and the school summer holidays, with September also benefiting from late-season visitors.

3. Evidence on price sensitivity
In the last week of June 2025 we raised the weekend BAR by £10, from £135 to the current £145. Weekend occupancy in July rose to 89%, from 81% in June. This tells us that our weekend guests are not price sensitive at current levels; if anything, the higher rate appears to have reinforced our positioning as a quality option, and we expect the further increase to be absorbed in the same way.

This is consistent with feedback from our guest satisfaction surveys, where weekend guests rate "value for money" at 8.4 out of 10, the highest score among our competitive set.

4. Two-night minimum
Saturday nights are our most constrained inventory: we sold out on 31 Saturdays in 2025. Many of these guests stay only one night, leaving rooms empty on Friday or Sunday either side. A two-night minimum for stays including a Saturday will convert single-night Saturday stays into two-night stays and smooth occupancy across the weekend.

Our booking data show that weddings at Quayside Hall, the venue next door, account for around 38% of our Saturday-night room bookings. Wedding guests typically book as a block through the couple, arrive on the Saturday afternoon and check out on the Sunday morning.

5. Revenue impact
Across our 124 rooms, 104 weekend nights a year and average weekend occupancy of 79%, a £20 increase in BAR is worth about £204,000 a year in additional room revenue, before any gain from longer stays. We have assumed weekend occupancy is maintained at 2025 levels, which we consider prudent given the evidence above.

The two-night minimum should add further revenue through additional Friday and Sunday nights. We have not quantified this but expect it to be material, particularly in shoulder months.

6. Implementation and monitoring
The new rates will be loaded into the channel manager on 15 May for stays from 1 June, giving online travel agencies two weeks' notice. Corporate contracted rates and group rates already contracted will be honoured. We will review pick-up weekly against the same weeks in 2025 and report to the General Manager monthly. If weekend occupancy for any month falls more than five points below 2025, we will review the rate.

7. Recommendation
The evidence shows that our weekend guests are not price sensitive at current rates and that we are priced well below our competitive set. We recommend approval of the £165 weekend BAR and the two-night Saturday minimum from 1 June 2026, delivering at least £204,000 of additional annual room revenue.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [inconsistency] at: "Across our 124 rooms, 104 weekend nights a year and average weekend occupancy of 79%" -- The hotel is described as a 112-room hotel in the Context section, but the revenue estimate uses 124 rooms. With 112 rooms the same calculation gives 112 x 104 x 0.79 x £20 = about £184,000, not £204,000.
2. [unsupported_causal] at: "This tells us that our weekend guests are not price sensitive at current levels" -- The only evidence is that occupancy rose from June to July after a June rate rise, but the document itself says July and August are the strongest months because of the harbour festival and school holidays. The seasonal rise confounds the comparison; it cannot show demand is price-insensitive (let alone that the higher price helped).
3. [missing_consideration] at: "We have assumed weekend occupancy is maintained at 2025 levels, which we consider prudent given the evidence above." -- The document states that about 38% of Saturday-night bookings are wedding guests from the adjacent venue who stay only Saturday night. A two-night minimum would exclude or deter this group, but the revenue case assumes occupancy is maintained and never addresses the loss of these single-night Saturday bookings.

REVIEW:
The proposal may well be right that Harbourside is underpriced at weekends. But the evidence it leans on hardest doesn't show what it claims, and the revenue figure contains an error and several optimistic assumptions. The figure is not a floor.

## What checks out

- **Competitor gap:** £145 is £20–£35 below the set's £165–£180, as stated.
- **Average occupancy:** the 2025 monthly figures do average 79% (950 / 12).
- **Revenue arithmetic:** 124 × 104 × 0.79 × £20 = £203,758, matching the £204,000. But see point 2.
- **Monitoring:** comparing weekly pick-up against the same weeks of 2025 is the right comparison.

## Major issues

**1. The "direct test" of price sensitivity is a seasonal effect.**
Occupancy rose from 81% in June to 89% in July. But Table 1 itself shows July and August as the peak months, driven by the harbour festival and school holidays. Occupancy would be expected to rise in July whatever the price did. There are two further problems:

- **Booking lead times.** The rate changed in the last week of June, so much of July's business was probably already booked at £135. Many of the guests who made up July's occupancy never saw the new price.
- **Comparison needed.** A meaningful test would compare July–December 2025 with the same months of 2024, at the old rate. The proposal doesn't include 2024 data.

As it stands, the evidence neither shows nor rules out price sensitivity. The recommendation's claim that "the evidence shows that our weekend guests are not price sensitive" is not supported.

**2. The room count is wrong.**
Section 2 gives 112 rooms. Section 5 calculates on 124. On 112 rooms the same calculation gives about **£184,000**, which is £20,000 lower.

**3. The £20 applies only to rooms sold at BAR.**
The calculation applies the increase to every occupied weekend room. Much weekend business isn't sold at BAR:

- **Wedding blocks**, which are about 38% of Saturday bookings.
- **Contracted group and corporate rates.** The proposal honours these, so they don't rise.
- **Packages and other negotiated rates.**

Rooms sold through online travel agencies also lose commission on the £20, typically 15–20%. And if revenue is reported net of VAT, £20 on the room rate is about £16.67.

If, for example, 60% of weekend room-nights are sold at BAR, the gross gain on 112 rooms is roughly £110,000, and less again after VAT and commission. The true BAR share should come from the booking system.

**4. "Assumes no occupancy gain" really assumes no occupancy loss.**
The author presents the estimate as conservative. In fact it assumes zero response to a 14% price rise, which is the most optimistic assumption available. Two points help put this in perspective:

- **Break-even.** Ignoring lost spend on food, drink and parking, a £145 → £165 rise pays for itself unless BAR occupancy falls by more than about 12%, roughly 9–10 points from 79%. Counting lost ancillary spend lowers that threshold.
- **Uneven risk across the year.** The risk is lowest on the 31 sold-out Saturdays and highest in January–March, when weekend occupancy was 62–74%. A uniform year-round rise ignores this.

**5. The two-night minimum may cost revenue, not add it.**
Section 4 states two facts:
- Wedding guests are about 38% of Saturday bookings.
- They typically stay Saturday night only.

A two-night minimum applies directly to those guests. Contracted blocks are protected, but future wedding parties would be required to book two nights or go elsewhere. The policy could also strain the relationship with Quayside Hall. Single-night leisure guests may likewise book competitors that have no minimum.

On sold-out Saturdays, replacing one-night stays with two-night stays may be a gain. On the 21 Saturdays that didn't sell out, the minimum mainly turns business away. The author's claim that £204,000 is "a floor" because the minimum is unvalued doesn't follow. The minimum could be positive or negative.

## Smaller points

- **Year one will fall short of the annualised figure.** Bookings for June–August already made at £145 will be honoured, and summer and wedding business is booked well ahead.
- **The value-for-money score was measured at £145.** A score of 8.4 shows guests think the hotel is good value at that price. It doesn't show they'll pay £165, and the score will likely fall after the rise.
- **"Below competitors" stops being true.** At £165 the hotel matches the cheapest competitor, so it would be in line with the set rather than below it. The author's own description gets this right.
- **The monitoring trigger lags.** By the time a month's occupancy is known to be 5 points down, the following months are largely booked. Weekly pick-up pace should be the main trigger, with the monthly figure as a backstop.

## Suggested revisions

1. **Correct the room count** to 112.
2. **Restate the revenue estimate** using the actual share of weekend room-nights sold at BAR, net of commission and on the hotel's VAT basis. Add a scenario with a 3–5 point fall in occupancy, alongside the break-even figure.
3. **Replace the June–July comparison** with a year-on-year comparison of July–December 2024 against July–December 2025.
4. **Apply the rise selectively.** Consider raising the rate on high-demand dates (summer, festival and sold-out Saturdays) and holding it in January–March, rather than across the whole year.
5. **Limit the two-night minimum** to high-demand Saturdays, exclude wedding weekends at Quayside Hall, and estimate how many Saturday bookings it would turn away.

The underlying case for moving closer to the competitive set may be sound. With these changes, the proposal would show an expected gain that is real but smaller than £204,000. It would also show the risks plainly, rather than presenting the change as risk-free.
